course_description:
This course will critically discuss and analyse the nature and causes of conflict and various theories of dispute resolution to better equip legal practitioners and stakeholders in their roles as dispute resolvers and advisers. The course will examine dispute resolution processes used in civil, criminal and international contexts.

The course provides an overview of the major dispute resolution processes used in the Australian justice system, with a focus on non-litigious approaches. These include negotiation, facilitation, mediation, conciliation, case appraisal, arbitration and restorative practices. Each process is examined in terms of its purpose, theoretical justifications, and role within the broader justice system, with comparative analysis used to surface the assumptions and trade-offs underlying process design and selection.

At a deeper level, the course engages with the theoretical frameworks that shape how conflict is understood and how disputes are resolved, including interest-based, rights-based and power-based models, and critical perspectives on Western legal concepts such as rule of law, adversarial justice and access to justice. The course also explores how culture shapes both the experience of conflict and the legitimacy of resolution processes, with particular attention to First Nations perspectives on conflict and resolution. Emerging areas of theory and practice, including complex and public conflict, online dispute resolution and the use of AI in dispute resolution, are also examined.

LAWS7841 is an interactive course taught in seminar mode, and includes class discussion, role-play simulations, and reflective practice. It is designed to build theoretical foundations rather than develop procedural skills. While interactive practice is a central element, its purpose is to develop students’ capacity to analyse, evaluate and reflect on dispute resolution as a field of practice, rather than teach particular process models in detail. The course provides a rigorous foundation for legal practitioners and other professionals who work with people in conflict, including those in human resources, consulting, social work and government.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

This course aims to:

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate knowledge of dispute resolution theory from different disciplinary and cultural perspectives.
Reflect critically on the theoretical assumptions underlying dispute resolution practice and how those assumptions shape process design, practitioner conduct, and skills training.
Explain the nature, advantages and disadvantages of various dispute resolution processes, from both a theoretical and a practical perspective.
Analyse practical, legal and ethical issues that arise in dispute resolution.
Critically evaluate the selection of an appropriate type of dispute resolution process according to the circumstances of a particular case.

assessment_details.title: Dispute Resolution Proposal Presentation
assessment_details.task_description: Group presentation 40% (10 minutes plus approximately 5 minutes Q&A) This is a team-based group presentation and will be discussed in the first seminar. In Seminar Weekend One, you will form a small group (4-5 students) to work together on the presentation. You may choose your own group members. Your task is to develop a proposal for a dispute resolution process to facilitate resolution of a conflict scenario. Different conflict scenarios will be made available on Learn.UQ (Blackboard). Your team has to choose one of the scenarios to work on and develop a proposal for how to facilitate dispute resolution for that scenario. Please note that not all possible DR processes that you may choose will have been discussed when this presentation is due. This means that you have to engage in independent reading for subsequent modules to be able to choose the appropriate DR process. You are welcome to contact the Course Coordinator with any questions you have and to discuss your approach. You need to prepare a 10-minute team presentation to convince the stakeholder that your approach is appropriate and will assist in constructive engagement with the conflict. Explain why the suggested process is suitable for the particular conflict, what its advantages and disadvantages are and how you are going to deal with potential challenges and impasses. Identify and critically evaluated the theoretical assumptions underpinning your recommended process. Present a well-rounded proposal, which acknowledges weaknesses and challenges but also makes a persuasive argument based on the merits of the process chosen and its underlying theories. Innovation and engaging interactive presentations are encouraged. Following your presentation, there will be 5 minutes of Q&A. All presentations will be conducted on Zoom. Due date In class, you will be shown how to book a session for your group presentation, to be delivered online via Zoom. Session times will be available for week 7 (11-13 September) or week 8 (18-20 September). Exact dates and times for presentations TBC, depending on student enrolment numbers. Format Each oral presentation session will be approximately 2 hours, to allow multiple groups to present in one session. All group members must be present for the session. Your group will be presenting to the course coordinator and a small group of fellow students. The presentation will be recorded. Group input All group members must contribute to selecting, developing, researching, and presenting the topic. Every group member will receive the same mark, unless a case is made otherwise. Resources to support your group work will be provided on the course Blackboard and discussed in class. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Seminars Seminar topics are: Seminar 1 – Foundations: Understanding Conflict and Dispute Resolution Module 1: Understanding conflict: Course overview; Disciplinary and theoretical frameworks for understanding conflict and dispute resolution Module 2: Development of dispute resolution: The development of dispute resolution in Australia; Values and goals of dispute resolution; Facilitative, advisory and determinative processes; Interest-based, rights-based and power-based models as an analytical framework Seminar 2 - Core Dispute Resolution Processes: Negotiation, Mediation and Advisory Processes Module 3: Negotiation: Negotiation as the foundation for constructive conflict resolution; Distributive and integrative approaches to negotiation; Analytical frameworks for negotiation; The theory and practice of principled negotiation Module 4: Mediation and conciliation: Mediation - concepts, definitions, and theoretical approaches; Facilitative, evaluative and transformative models compared; Conciliation and other advisory processes Seminar 3 – Determinative Processes and the Legal and Ethical Dimensions of Dispute Resolution Module 5: Determinative processes and the legal architecture of dispute resolution: Arbitration - history, domestic and international arbitration, theoretical underpinnings, and critiques; Legal issues arising in DR: Confidentiality, practitioner conduct, liability and enforceability of outcomes; Integration of DR into justice systems – dispute systems design theory and process selection Module 6: Power, ethics and the limits of neutrality: Party autonomy, voluntariness, and the critique of mandatory DR; Power, neutrality, and impartiality -theoretical frameworks and practitioner implications; Ethics, standards of practice and practitioner accountability Seminar 4 – Culture, Context and Emerging Directions Module 7: The role of culture in dispute resolution: Culture and conflict – understanding the cultural underpinnings of dispute resolution; Critical analysis of Eurocentric approaches; First Nations perspectives on conflict and resolution; Restorative practices Module 8: Frontiers of dispute resolution: Technology, innovation and access to justice, including ODR and AI in dispute resolution; Complex, public and international conflict – value disputes, facilitating public dialogue, international and transitional justice; Critical synthesis and reflection on dispute resolution as an evolving field. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
